title: Hash Tables — Fast Lookups in Constant Time
text:
A hash table is one of the most widely used data structures in computer science, prized for its ability to store and retrieve data in average-case O(1) time. At its core, a hash table maps keys to values by using a hash function — a mathematical formula that converts a key into an index within an internal array.

When you insert a key-value pair, the hash function computes an index from the key. The value is then stored at that position in the array. To look up a value later, the same hash function is applied to the key, producing the same index, and the value is retrieved directly — no scanning required.

The critical challenge is handling collisions: situations where two different keys produce the same index. Two common strategies address this. Chaining stores a linked list at each array slot, so multiple entries can coexist at the same index. Open addressing, on the other hand, probes for the next empty slot when a collision occurs, using patterns like linear probing or quadratic probing.

The quality of the hash function matters enormously. A good hash function distributes keys uniformly across the array, minimising collisions. A poor one clusters keys together, degrading performance toward O(n) in the worst case. Cryptographic hash functions like SHA-256 provide excellent distribution but are slower; simpler functions like polynomial rolling hashes are faster for everyday use.

Hash tables also need to resize. As the ratio of stored entries to array size (the load factor) grows past a threshold — typically around 0.75 — the table allocates a larger array and rehashes every entry. This operation is expensive but infrequent, keeping amortised insertion cost at O(1).

Real-world applications are everywhere: Python dictionaries, JavaScript objects, database indexes, caches, and symbol tables in compilers all rely on hash tables for their speed.

title: TCP Three-Way Handshake — Establishing Reliable Connections
text:
The Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) is the backbone of reliable communication on the internet. Before any data flows between a client and server, TCP establishes a connection through a process called the three-way handshake, which ensures both sides are ready to communicate and agree on initial parameters.

The handshake begins when the client sends a SYN (synchronise) segment to the server. This segment contains a randomly chosen initial sequence number (ISN), which TCP uses to track the order of bytes in the data stream. The sequence number is random rather than starting at zero for security — predictable numbers could allow attackers to hijack connections.

The server receives the SYN and responds with a SYN-ACK segment. This segment acknowledges the client's sequence number by setting the acknowledgement field to the client's ISN plus one. Simultaneously, the server includes its own randomly chosen ISN, effectively saying: "I received your request and here is my starting number."

Finally, the client sends an ACK segment back to the server, acknowledging the server's sequence number. At this point, the connection is considered established, and both sides can begin transmitting application data. This final ACK can actually carry data payload, saving a round trip in practice.

The three-way handshake solves several problems. It confirms that both endpoints are reachable and willing to communicate. It synchronises sequence numbers so both sides can detect missing, duplicated, or out-of-order segments. It also prevents stale connection requests from previous sessions from being mistakenly accepted — a problem known as the "old duplicate" issue.

When either side is finished, TCP uses a four-step teardown process involving FIN and ACK segments. This graceful shutdown ensures all data has been delivered before the connection closes.

title: Binary Search — Efficient Searching in Sorted Data
text:
Binary search is a fundamental algorithm that finds a target value within a sorted array by repeatedly halving the search space. While a linear scan checks every element one by one in O(n) time, binary search achieves O(log n) time complexity, making it dramatically faster on large datasets.

The algorithm maintains two pointers — low and high — that define the current search range. At each step, it computes the middle index and compares the element there to the target. If the middle element matches the target, the search is complete. If the target is smaller, the search continues in the left half by moving the high pointer to mid minus one. If the target is larger, it continues in the right half by moving the low pointer to mid plus one.

This halving process is remarkably efficient. An array of one million elements requires at most twenty comparisons, since log₂(1,000,000) is approximately twenty. An array of one billion elements needs only thirty. This logarithmic scaling is what makes binary search indispensable.

However, binary search has a strict prerequisite: the data must be sorted. If the array is unsorted, you must sort it first, which costs O(n log n) — worthwhile only if you plan to search multiple times. For a single search on unsorted data, linear scan is actually more efficient.

A common pitfall is integer overflow when computing the midpoint. The naive formula (low + high) / 2 can overflow if low and high are both large. The safe alternative is low + (high - low) / 2, which avoids the issue entirely.

Beyond simple lookup, binary search underpins many algorithms: finding insertion points, locating boundaries in sorted ranges, searching in rotated arrays, and optimising monotonic functions. Libraries like Python's bisect module and C++'s lower_bound are built on binary search.

title: Database Indexing — How B-Trees Speed Up Queries
text:
When a database table holds millions of rows, finding a specific record without an index requires a full table scan — reading every row until the match is found. Database indexes solve this by creating auxiliary data structures that allow the database engine to locate rows in logarithmic time, much like a book's index helps you find a topic without reading every page.

The most common index structure is the B-tree (balanced tree). A B-tree is a self-balancing tree where each node can hold multiple keys and pointers. Unlike a binary tree, which has at most two children per node, a B-tree node may have hundreds or thousands of children. This high branching factor keeps the tree shallow — typically three to four levels deep even for tables with billions of rows — so lookups require only a few disk reads.

When you create an index on a column, the database builds a B-tree whose keys are the column values and whose leaf nodes contain pointers to the actual rows on disk. A query like SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'alice@example.com' traverses the B-tree from root to leaf, reading perhaps three or four pages instead of millions.

Indexes accelerate not just exact-match lookups but also range queries (WHERE age BETWEEN 20 AND 30) because B-tree leaves are linked in sorted order. The database walks the leaf chain between the two boundary values.

However, indexes come with trade-offs. Each index consumes storage space, and every INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE must update both the table and all its indexes, slowing write operations. Over-indexing a table with rarely queried columns wastes resources. The general guideline is to index columns that appear frequently in WHERE clauses, JOIN conditions, and ORDER BY clauses.

Composite indexes on multiple columns (e.g., last_name, first_name) follow a leftmost-prefix rule: the index is usable only when the query filters on a prefix of the indexed columns.

title: CPU Cache — Bridging the Processor-Memory Speed Gap
text:
Modern processors execute instructions at speeds measured in gigahertz, but main memory (DRAM) is far slower — a single memory access can take hundreds of CPU cycles. Without a solution, the processor would spend most of its time idle, waiting for data. CPU caches bridge this gap by keeping frequently accessed data in small, extremely fast memory located directly on the processor chip.

Caches are organised in a hierarchy of levels. The L1 cache is the smallest (typically 32-64 KB per core) and the fastest, with access times of just one to four cycles. The L2 cache is larger (256 KB to 1 MB) but slightly slower. The L3 cache, shared among all cores, can be several megabytes but takes ten to forty cycles to access. When the processor needs data, it checks each level in order; a hit at any level avoids the expensive trip to main memory.

Cache performance depends on two types of locality. Temporal locality means that recently accessed data is likely to be accessed again soon — think of a loop variable. Spatial locality means that data stored near a recently accessed address is likely needed next — think of iterating through an array. Cache hardware exploits both by fetching data in blocks called cache lines (typically 64 bytes), so neighbouring data comes along for free.

When the cache is full and new data must be loaded, an eviction policy decides which existing data to discard. The Least Recently Used (LRU) policy is the most common, evicting the data that has not been accessed for the longest time.

Understanding caches explains many performance puzzles. Accessing a two-dimensional array row-by-row is faster than column-by-column because row-major storage matches spatial locality. Poorly structured data access patterns — cache thrashing — can degrade performance by orders of magnitude, even when the algorithm's time complexity is unchanged.

title: Recursion — Solving Problems by Self-Reference
text:
Recursion is a programming technique where a function calls itself to solve a problem by breaking it into smaller, identical sub-problems. Rather than describing step-by-step instructions with loops, recursion expresses solutions declaratively: define what happens in the simplest case, then describe how to reduce any larger case to a simpler one.

Every recursive function requires two components. The base case is the simplest version of the problem that can be answered directly, without further recursion — it prevents infinite self-calls. The recursive case breaks the current problem into one or more smaller instances and calls the function on those. For example, computing factorial: factorial(0) = 1 is the base case, and factorial(n) = n × factorial(n - 1) is the recursive case.

When a function calls itself, the computer pushes a new frame onto the call stack, storing the function's local variables and the return address. Each recursive call adds a frame; each return removes one. If the recursion goes too deep without reaching a base case, the stack overflows — the dreaded stack overflow error. Most languages set a default recursion limit (Python's is 1000) to prevent this.

Recursion is naturally suited to problems with recursive structure: tree traversal, divide-and-conquer algorithms like merge sort, parsing nested expressions, and exploring combinations or permutations. The same problems can often be solved iteratively, but the recursive version is frequently clearer and easier to reason about.

However, naive recursion can be inefficient. Computing Fibonacci numbers recursively without memoisation creates an exponential explosion of redundant calls. Dynamic programming addresses this by storing previously computed results (memoisation) so each sub-problem is solved only once, reducing exponential time to polynomial.

Tail recursion is a special form where the recursive call is the last operation in the function. Some languages (Scheme, Haskell, and others) optimise tail calls by reusing the current stack frame, eliminating stack growth entirely.

title: Public Key Cryptography — Securing Communication with Asymmetric Keys
text:
Public key cryptography solved one of the oldest problems in secure communication: how can two parties who have never met agree on a secret without an eavesdropper learning it? Before its invention in the 1970s, both sender and receiver needed to share the same secret key in advance — a logistical nightmare at internet scale.

The breakthrough idea is to use a pair of mathematically linked keys instead of one. The public key can be shared openly; the private key must be kept secret. Data encrypted with the public key can only be decrypted with the corresponding private key, and vice versa. This asymmetry eliminates the need to exchange secrets over insecure channels.

RSA, one of the earliest and most widely used algorithms, relies on the difficulty of factoring large numbers. Two large primes are multiplied to produce a modulus; the public and private keys are derived from this modulus and the primes. Encrypting a message is fast (modular exponentiation), but breaking the encryption without the private key requires factoring the modulus — a problem that remains computationally infeasible for sufficiently large keys (2048 bits or more).

Public key cryptography enables several essential operations. Encryption ensures confidentiality: only the holder of the private key can read the message. Digital signatures provide authenticity and integrity: signing with the private key creates a signature that anyone can verify with the public key, confirming the sender's identity and that the message was not altered.

In practice, asymmetric encryption is slow compared to symmetric algorithms like AES. Therefore, most protocols use a hybrid approach: the public key encrypts a random session key, and the session key encrypts the actual data using a fast symmetric cipher. TLS, which secures web traffic, uses exactly this pattern.

Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) offers the same security as RSA with much smaller keys, making it preferred for mobile and embedded devices.

title: REST API Design — Principles of Scalable Web Services
text:
REST (Representational State Transfer) is an architectural style for designing web APIs that has become the dominant standard for communication between client applications and servers. Proposed by Roy Fielding in his 2000 doctoral dissertation, REST builds on the existing infrastructure of HTTP and the web, rather than inventing new protocols.

The central abstraction in REST is the resource — any piece of information that can be named. Users, products, orders, and articles are all resources. Each resource is identified by a unique URI (Uniform Resource Identifier), such as /api/users/42. Clients interact with resources by sending HTTP requests using standard methods: GET retrieves a resource, POST creates a new one, PUT replaces an existing one, PATCH updates it partially, and DELETE removes it.

A key REST constraint is statelessness: each request from the client must contain all the information the server needs to process it. The server does not store session state between requests. This design simplifies scaling because any server in a cluster can handle any request — there is no need to route a client to a specific server that holds its session.

Resources are represented in a transfer format, most commonly JSON. The client and server negotiate the representation through HTTP content-type headers. A single resource — say, a user — can have multiple representations (JSON, XML, HTML) depending on what the client requests.

Proper use of HTTP status codes is essential for a well-designed REST API. 200 means success, 201 indicates a resource was created, 400 signals a client error, 404 means the resource was not found, and 500 indicates a server error.

HATEOAS (Hypermedia as the Engine of Application State) is an advanced REST constraint where the server's responses include links to related actions, allowing clients to navigate the API dynamically rather than hardcoding URLs.

Good REST APIs are versioned (e.g., /api/v1/users), paginated for large collections, and documented with tools like OpenAPI (Swagger).
